title: Starting a Basic Care Facility in North Dakota: Licensing, Costs, and Step-by-Step Guide

html:
Introduction

Starting a Basic Care Facility in North Dakota represents a meaningful opportunity to serve seniors and adults with impaired capacity requiring housing, personal care, and supportive services while building a compliant, sustainable care business. This venture allows entrepreneurs to address a critical need within the state’s healthcare continuum, providing a safe and supportive environment for a vulnerable population. Oversight and funding are administered by the North Dakota Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), which is the primary state agency responsible for licensing and regulation. For providers seeking to serve lower-income residents, reimbursement and program funding are coordinated through the state’s Medicaid program, also managed by HHS.

With strong demand for specialized services like memory care, behavioral health support, and transitional care, and a defined Medicaid reimbursement structure offering approximately $158.69 per day (as of July 2023), North Dakota offers a structured market with clear opportunities for providers prepared to navigate licensing, staffing, and compliance requirements. This clear financial framework, combined with identified market gaps, creates a promising landscape for new facilities that can deliver high-quality, specialized care. Success hinges on a deep understanding of the regulatory environment and a commitment to operational excellence.

This guide walks you through every step of launching a Basic Care Facility in North Dakota, from understanding state regulations and licensing procedures to developing a business plan, hiring staff, and preparing for your first inspection. Whether you are acquiring an existing facility or building from the ground up, this comprehensive overview will provide the roadmap you need to achieve licensure and build a successful care business.

Table of Contents

  • Understand North Dakota’s Basic Care Facility Regulations
  • Choose the Type and Size of Your Program
  • Business Structure and Licensing
  • Develop a Comprehensive Business Plan
  • Secure a Suitable Facility or Office
  • Hire and Train Qualified Staff
  • Policies, Procedures, and Care Plans
  • Marketing and Referral Development
  • Maintain Compliance and Prepare for Reviews
  • Frequently Asked Questions

Section 1: Understand North Dakota’s Basic Care Facility Regulations

Before you can lay the foundation for your business, you must first understand the regulatory landscape. North Dakota regulates Basic Care Facilities through the North Dakota Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), which is responsible for the licensing and oversight of facilities providing housing, room, board, and health, social, or personal care to five or more residents. These regulations are outlined in the North Dakota Century Code, specifically Chapter 23-09.3, which defines the scope of care, operational standards, and enforcement actions.

Providers serving Medicaid-eligible populations must also comply with federal frameworks, primarily the rules set by the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS), which govern reimbursement and quality standards for state Medicaid programs. Additionally, all providers must adhere to the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) to protect resident health information. The state’s regulatory framework emphasizes resident safety, quality of life, and the appropriate delivery of personal and supportive care services. This includes detailed requirements for resident rights, physical environment safety, proper medication management, comprehensive documentation, and robust quality oversight. Licenses are not a one-time achievement; they require renewal every one year, contingent upon a successful annual inspection and continued compliance.

Navigating these layers of state and federal rules can be complex. A thorough review of the Century Code and HHS guidelines is the essential first step for any prospective owner. Understanding these rules upfront will inform every subsequent decision, from your business plan and facility design to your staffing model and operational policies.

Section 2: Choose the Type and Size of Your Program

Once you have a grasp of the regulations, your next step is to define the specific service niche and scale of your operation. While North Dakota primarily licenses ‘Basic Care Facilities,’ providers often specialize to meet specific market needs and differentiate themselves. The state’s market data shows high demand for facilities that offer more than just standard room and board.

North Dakota supports multiple Basic Care Facility variants, each with different staffing, training, and programming requirements:

  • Standard Basic Care: This model serves the general population of seniors and adults who need assistance with activities of daily living (ADLs) like bathing, dressing, and medication reminders but do not require 24/7 skilled nursing care.
  • Memory Care Unit: These are often specialized, secured wings within a larger facility or standalone buildings designed for residents with Alzheimer’s disease or other forms of dementia. They require enhanced staff training in dementia care, specialized activity programming, and environmental modifications to ensure safety.
  • Behavioral Health Focused Care: This specialization caters to residents with specific behavioral or mental health needs that may not be adequately managed in a traditional setting. It requires staff trained in de-escalation and behavioral support, along with close coordination with mental health professionals.
  • Transitional Care Programs: These programs offer short-term stays for individuals who are discharged from a hospital but are not yet ready to return home. They focus on rehabilitation, medication reconciliation, and ensuring a safe transition back to the community.

Program size in North Dakota must serve a minimum of five residents. Beyond that, capacity typically ranges from 10 to 60 beds or more, depending on the business model and facility size. Demand is strongest in urban centers like Fargo, Bismarck, Grand Forks, and Minot, where population density and healthcare infrastructure are concentrated. However, rural counties may present opportunities due to less competition, though providers in these areas must carefully assess workforce availability and proximity to referral sources like hospitals.

Section 3: Business Structure and Licensing

With your program type and target market defined, it’s time to formalize your business and begin the official licensing process. A solid legal and administrative foundation is critical for long-term success and compliance. Providers in North Dakota typically operate as a Limited Liability Company (LLC) or S-Corporation to protect personal assets from business liabilities.

To become a licensed provider, you must complete several key administrative steps:

  • Register Your Business: File articles of organization (for an LLC) or incorporation (for a corporation) with the North Dakota Secretary of State.
  • Obtain an EIN: Apply for an Employer Identification Number (EIN) from the IRS. This is required for tax purposes and for hiring employees.
  • Secure Insurance: Obtain necessary insurance coverage, including general liability, professional liability (errors and omissions), and workers’ compensation insurance.
  • Submit a Licensing Application: The core of the process is submitting a complete and accurate licensing application to the North Dakota Department of Health and Human Services (HHS). This application package is extensive and requires detailed information about your business structure, ownership, key personnel, facility details, and operational plans.

Licensing timelines in North Dakota generally range from 6 to 12 months. This timeframe can be influenced by the completeness of your application, the need for any construction or renovation to bring your facility into compliance, and the HHS inspection schedule. Delays are often caused by incomplete paperwork, missing policies, or facility issues discovered during the initial review. Careful preparation is key to a smooth and timely approval.

Section 4: Develop a Comprehensive Business Plan

A robust business plan is your blueprint for success, serving as both an internal guide and a crucial document for securing financing. Your plan should detail every aspect of your operation, from startup costs to long-term profitability projections.

Startup costs for a Basic Care Facility in North Dakota typically range from $300,000 to $1,500,000. This wide range depends on whether you are leasing, buying, or building a facility, as well as the extent of renovations and equipment needed. Key startup expenses include real estate acquisition/down payment, licensing and consultation fees, furniture and fixtures, resident care equipment, and at least six months of operating capital.

Operating expenses are driven primarily by labor. Staffing represents 50-60% of total operating costs, making efficient scheduling and retention critical. Other major expenses include mortgage/rent, utilities, food, insurance, and supplies. Understanding your revenue model is equally important. Typical reimbursement or revenue ranges in North Dakota include:

  • Medicaid Basic Care Assistance: Approximately $158.69 per resident per day (as of July 2023). To accept this, you must become an enrolled Medicaid provider.
  • Private Pay: Rates for private-pay residents are typically higher and can range from $4,500 to $7,000 per month, depending on the room size, level of care required, and any specialized services (like memory care).
  • Annual Gross Revenue: Depending on facility size and occupancy, annual revenues can range from $500,000 to over $3,000,000.

Profitability is directly tied to occupancy. Providers operating at a target occupancy of 85-90% generally achieve gross profit margins in the 4-8% range. Most facilities plan for a break-even period of 18-24 months as they ramp up their census and stabilize operations.

Section 5: Secure a Suitable Facility or Office

The physical building is a cornerstone of your license and your ability to provide safe care. Your chosen facility must meet strict state and local codes before HHS will issue a license. Location selection should be a strategic decision that considers zoning regulations, accessibility for residents and families, proximity to hospitals and other referral sources, and the availability of a qualified local workforce.

Key facility requirements for a Basic Care Facility in North Dakota include:

  • Code Compliance: The building must comply with all state and local building, fire, and safety codes, with documentation of recent inspections.
  • Resident Rooms: Minimum square footage requirements must be met for resident rooms (e.g., typically 80 sq. ft. for a single-occupancy room and 60 sq. ft. per person in a multi-occupancy room).
  • Accessibility: Common areas, bathrooms, and entryways must be accessible to individuals with disabilities, adhering to ADA standards.
  • Dining and Kitchen: A dedicated dining area must be provided, along with a commercial-grade kitchen that meets public health standards for food service.
  • Medication Management: A secure, locked area for medication storage and a designated station for administration are required.
  • Environmental Systems: The facility must have adequate and functioning lighting, heating, and ventilation systems to ensure resident comfort and safety.

Whether you are renovating an existing building or constructing a new one, it is crucial to work with architects and contractors who are experienced with healthcare facility regulations to avoid costly mistakes and delays in your licensing timeline.

Section 6: Hire and Train Qualified Staff

Your staff is the heart of your facility. They deliver the hands-on care and create the supportive environment that defines your residents’ quality of life. North Dakota’s regulations mandate specific staffing roles and ratios to ensure resident needs are met safely and effectively. Hiring a compassionate, qualified, and compliant team is non-negotiable.

Required roles for a Basic Care Facility typically include:

  • Administrator: A licensed or qualified individual responsible for the overall day-to-day management of the facility, including compliance, finance, and staffing.
  • Registered Nurse (RN) or Licensed Practical Nurse (LPN): A licensed nurse is required to oversee health services, conduct resident assessments, and manage the medication administration program.
  • Direct Care Staff / Resident Aides: These are the frontline caregivers who provide hands-on assistance with activities of daily living, monitor residents, and document care.
  • Activities Director: An individual responsible for planning and implementing a robust calendar of social, recreational, and therapeutic activities to promote resident engagement and well-being.
  • Dietary Staff: This includes a cook and dietary aides responsible for planning, preparing, and serving nutritious meals that meet residents’ dietary needs and preferences.

All staff must undergo thorough background checks before hire. Training is another critical compliance point. Required training includes initial orientation on facility policies, resident rights, infection control, emergency procedures, dementia care (if applicable), and certification for medication assistance. Ongoing continuing education is also mandated to keep staff skills current and ensure they are up-to-date on best practices and regulatory changes.

Section 7: Policies, Procedures, and Care Plans

Comprehensive, written policies and procedures are the operational backbone of a licensed facility. These documents are not just for show; they are the rulebook that guides your staff, ensures consistent care delivery, and demonstrates compliance to state surveyors. During your licensing inspection, HHS will meticulously review your policy manual to ensure it meets all regulatory requirements.

North Dakota requires written policies covering a wide range of operational areas, including:

  • Admission, Transfer, and Discharge Criteria
  • Resident Rights and Grievance Procedures
  • Medication Management and Administration
  • Emergency and Disaster Preparedness Plan
  • Infection Control and Prevention
  • Staffing Plans, Job Descriptions, and Training
  • Care Planning and Resident Assessment Processes
  • Incident Reporting and Investigation

At the center of your documentation is the individual care or service plan. This person-centered document must be developed for each resident upon admission, based on a comprehensive assessment. It outlines the resident’s specific needs, preferences, and goals, and details the services your facility will provide to meet them. These plans must be reviewed and updated regularly (e.g., quarterly or with any significant change in condition) in accordance with North Dakota and federal rules.

Section 8: Marketing and Referral Development

Once your facility is licensed and ready to operate, your focus shifts to filling your beds. In the senior and healthcare industry, traditional consumer advertising is often less effective than building a strong professional referral network. Your reputation for quality care and compliance will be your most powerful marketing tool.

Referrals for Basic Care Facilities in North Dakota typically come from:

  • Hospital discharge planners and social workers
  • Skilled Nursing Facilities (SNFs) for residents stepping down in care level
  • Physician’s offices and specialty clinics (e.g., neurologists, geriatricians)
  • Home health and hospice agencies
  • Local Area Agencies on Aging
  • Online placement agencies and senior living directories

Successful providers focus on building trusted relationships with these key sources. This involves meeting with discharge planners to explain your specific services (e.g., memory care, transitional care), ensuring a smooth and responsive admission process, and providing excellent communication and outcome documentation. When a hospital social worker knows your facility is compliant, responsive, and capable of handling complex cases, you become their go-to solution. This B2B (business-to-business) approach generates a steady stream of qualified residents and is far more cost-effective than broad consumer marketing campaigns.

Section 9: Maintain Compliance and Prepare for Reviews

Receiving your license is the beginning, not the end, of your compliance journey. Oversight in North Dakota includes annual, unannounced inspections conducted by surveyors from the North Dakota Department of Health and Human Services (HHS). These inspections are thorough and cover every aspect of your operation, from resident records and medication carts to kitchen cleanliness and staff files.

Inspections are focused on identifying deficiencies, which are violations of state regulations. Common deficiencies found during surveys often relate to:

  • Incomplete or outdated resident care plans.
  • Medication administration errors or documentation gaps.
  • Inadequate staff training documentation or missing background checks.
  • Fire safety and environmental hazards (e.g., blocked exits, improper food storage, water temperature issues).
  • Failure to properly document and investigate resident incidents or grievances.

Avoiding these common pitfalls requires a commitment to continuous quality improvement. This means conducting your own internal audits, holding regular staff training, and maintaining audit-ready documentation at all times. When surveyors arrive, you should be able to confidently present organized records that demonstrate your ongoing commitment to resident safety and regulatory compliance. A proactive approach to quality assurance is the best way to ensure a smooth survey and maintain your license in good standing.

Section 10: Frequently Asked Questions

Q: How long does it take to open a Basic Care Facility in North Dakota?

A: The entire process, from business planning to receiving your first resident, typically takes 18-24 months. This includes time for securing financing, facility acquisition or renovation, and the formal licensing period with HHS, which itself can take 6-12 months.

Q: What licenses are required to open a Basic Care Facility in North Dakota?

A: You need a Basic Care Facility license issued by the North Dakota Department of Health and Human Services (HHS). This is mandated by North Dakota Century Code 23-09.3 for any facility providing room, board, and personal care services to five or more individuals.

Q: What reimbursement is available for Basic Care Facilities in North Dakota?

A: Reimbursement is available through two primary sources: private pay from residents and their families, and the state’s Medicaid Basic Care Assistance Program. As of July 2023, the Medicaid rate was approximately $158.69 per day. To accept Medicaid, providers must enroll with North Dakota’s Medicaid program.

Conclusion

Starting a Basic Care Facility in North Dakota is a challenging yet immensely rewarding endeavor. It requires careful planning, a deep understanding of state and federal regulations, and unwavering operational discipline. The market holds clear opportunities, particularly for providers who can deliver specialized memory care, behavioral health support, or transitional services. By focusing on compliance, investing in qualified staff, and building strong relationships with professional referral sources, you can position your facility for long-term success and make a profound impact on the lives of your residents.
